An infinite number of infinitesimally small compounding periods during a holding period is known as continuous compounding. The continuously compounded return is related to the holding period return; it is the natural log of the ratio of the ending value to the beginning value of the investment.
In this scenario, solve to determine the Year 1 continuously compounded return using the price at the beginning (St) and price at the end (St+1) of the one-year holding period, which are both given.
Note that the continuously compounded return in this scenario is lower than the holding period return (6.06%). This makes sense due to the fact that compounding at a lower rate more frequently results in the same return as compounding at a higher rate less frequently.
(Choice B) 6.06% is the Year 1 holding period return.
(Choice C) 6.41% is the geometric mean of the two-year, continuously compounded return.

With interest-bearing investments, lenders (investors) earn interest periodically (eg, monthly, quarterly) based on a specific periodic rate over time. When interest is compounded, interest income is reinvested each period at the periodic rate, so additional interest is earned on previous interest. Therefore, the total value of the investment (including principal and interest) grows at the periodic rate. The investment's percentage growth in annual terms, accounting for periodic compounding, is known as the effective annual rate (EAR).
The EAR is derived from the periodic rate. Since the periodic rate is not given, it must be derived from the stated annual rate (rs). The rs is an annualized quotation convention (used by financial institutions) that equals the periodic rate multiplied by the number of compounding periods per year (m). To derive the periodic rate, divide the rs by m.
Calculate EAR for the three loans:
The EAR for Loan Y is 10.97%. An EAR example illustrates how $1 invested today in Loan Y will result in an annual return of 10.97%.

The annualized rate of return is an application of the geometric mean return. It converts a holding period return to an equivalent annualized return. To find the annualized rate of return, determine the time unit (eg, days, months, or years). Identify how many time units occur in one year (eg, days = 365, months = 12, year = 1). Express the time in years. Apply this standardized unit of time to the geometric mean return formula.
